claim: The diploid-to-haploid life form transition is governed by the loss of H3K9me2 and DNA demethylation of transposon-associated cis-regulatory elements.
source: The diploid-to-haploid life form transition is governed by the loss of H3K9me2 and DNA demethylation of transposon-associated cis-regulatory elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented throughout the manuscript, including ATAC-seq, ChIP-seq, and DNA methylation analysis showing loss of H3K9me2 and DNA demethylation in the vegetative cell.

claim: The diploid-to-haploid transition is associated with dramatic changes in chromatin accessibility and transcriptional reprogramming.
source: This event is associated with dramatic changes in chromatin accessibility and transcriptional reprogramming.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and RNA-seq data comparing microspores, vegetative cells, and sperm nuclei.

claim: The global loss of H3K27me3 in the haploid form shapes a chromatin accessibility landscape that is poised to re-initiate the transition back to diploid life after fertilisation.
source: In contrast, the global loss of H3K27me3 in the haploid form shapes a chromatin accessibility landscape that is poised to re-initiate the transition back to diploid life after fertilisation.
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data showing accessible chromatin at embryonic regulators in sperm, and ChIP-seq data showing loss of H3K27me3.

claim: DNA and histone methylation are reprogrammed during germline differentiation and after fertilisation to reconfigure transcription in the mammalian embryo.
source: DNA and histone methylation are reprogrammed during germline differentiation and after fertilisation to reconfigure transcription in the mammalian embryo (Hajkova, 2011; Reik et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In plants and algae, meiosis marks the transition from the diploid sporophyte to haploid gamete-producing gametophytes.
source: In plants and algae, meiosis marks the transition from the diploid sporophyte to haploid gamete-producing gametophytes, while the union of gametes at fertilisation re-initiates the transition back to the diploid phase (Hackenberg and Twell, 2019; Haig, 2008; Hisanaga et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on plant life cycles.

claim: The union of gametes at fertilisation re-initiates the transition back to the diploid phase in plants and algae.
source: In plants and algae, meiosis marks the transition from the diploid sporophyte to haploid gamete-producing gametophytes, while the union of gametes at fertilisation re-initiates the transition back to the diploid phase (Hackenberg and Twell, 2019; Haig, 2008; Hisanaga et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to established literature on plant life cycles.

claim: Marked differences in development, morphology, and gene expression exist between the gametophyte and sporophyte.
source: The marked differences in development, morphology, and gene expression between the gametophyte and sporophyte (Borg et al., 2009; Couceiro et al., 2015; Dickinson and Grant-Downton, 2009; Heesch et al., 2019) suggest that epigenetic patterns are reprogrammed between these two life forms.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies documenting these differences.

claim: Epigenetic patterns are reprogrammed between the gametophyte and sporophyte life forms.
source: The marked differences in development, morphology, and gene expression between the gametophyte and sporophyte (Borg et al., 2009; Couceiro et al., 2015; Dickinson and Grant-Downton, 2009; Heesch et al., 2019) suggest that epigenetic patterns are reprogrammed between these two life forms.
evidence: This is inferred from the marked differences in development, morphology, and gene expression between life forms.

claim: Ancestral land plants represented by extant bryophytes typically have a dominant haploid gametophytic phase.
source: Ancestral land plants represented by extant bryophytes typically have a dominant haploid gametophytic phase and require Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) activity to repress precocious sporophyte development (Okano et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research on bryophyte development.

claim: Bryophytes require Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) activity to repress precocious sporophyte development.
source: Ancestral land plants represented by extant bryophytes typically have a dominant haploid gametophytic phase and require Polycomb Repressive Complex 2 (PRC2) activity to repress precocious sporophyte development (Okano et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DNA methylation undergoes extensive reprogramming between the haploid and diploid phase in bryophytes.
source: DNA methylation also undergoes extensive reprogramming between the haploid and diploid phase in bryophytes, although it remains unclear whether this is required for the transitions between the two life forms (Ikeda et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2018; Yaari et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies on bryophyte DNA methylation.

claim: It remains unclear whether DNA methylation reprogramming is required for the transitions between haploid and diploid life forms in bryophytes.
source: DNA methylation also undergoes extensive reprogramming between the haploid and diploid phase in bryophytes, although it remains unclear whether this is required for the transitions between the two life forms (Ikeda et al., 2018; Schmid et al., 2018; Yaari et al., 2015).
evidence: This represents a gap in current knowledge as stated in the manuscript.

claim: Flowering plants have a dominant diploid sporophytic phase that culminates with the production of meiotic spores from somatic tissue within the flower.
source: In contrast, flowering plants have a dominant diploid sporophytic phase that culminates with the production of meiotic spores from somatic tissue within the flower.
evidence: This is established knowledge about flowering plant life cycles.

claim: Haploid spores develop into multicellular male or female gametophytes depending on whether they originate in the anther or ovary, respectively.
source: Haploid spores develop into multicellular male or female gametophytes depending on whether they originate in the anther or ovary, respectively (Dickinson and Grant-Downton, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to established literature on plant development.

claim: The female gametophyte in flowering plants is comprised of an embryo sac containing the egg and accessory cells.
source: The female gametophyte in flowering plants is comprised of an embryo sac containing the egg and accessory cells (Erbasol Serbes et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Pollen represents the male gametophyte.
source: Pollen represents the male gametophyte.
evidence: This is established knowledge about plant reproduction.

claim: The germ cell represents the male germline initial cell and undergoes a distinct developmental programme to divide and differentiate into two sperms.
source: The germ cell represents the male germline initial cell and undergoes a distinct developmental programme to divide and differentiate into two sperms (Borg et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Sperm differentiation is intricately linked with epigenetic reprogramming of sperm chromatin in Arabidopsis.
source: Sperm differentiation is intricately linked with epigenetic reprogramming of sperm chromatin in Arabidopsis.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Targeted removal of repressive H3K27me3 marks from histone-based sperm chromatin facilitates the transcription of genes required for sperm differentiation, which are normally silenced by H3K27me3 during sporophytic life.
source: Targeted removal of repressive H3K27me3 marks from histone-based sperm chromatin facilitates the transcription of genes required for sperm differentiation, which are normally silenced by H3K27me3 during sporophytic life (Borg et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The vegetative cell represents the somatic cell of the male gametophyte.
source: The vegetative cell represents the somatic cell of the male gametophyte and undergoes loss of constitutive heterochromatin, which facilitates active DNA demethylation by DME (He et al., 2019; Mérai et al., 2014; Schoft et al., 2009; Schoft et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about pollen development.

claim: The vegetative cell undergoes loss of constitutive heterochromatin, which facilitates active DNA demethylation by DME.
source: The vegetative cell represents the somatic cell of the male gametophyte and undergoes loss of constitutive heterochromatin, which facilitates active DNA demethylation by DME (He et al., 2019; Mérai et al., 2014; Schoft et al., 2009; Schoft et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: VN chromatin organisation is highly diffuse compared to sperm nuclei and somatic cell nuclei.
source: VC nuclear (VN) chromatin organisation is highly diffuse compared to sperm nuclei (SN) and somatic cell nuclei (Borg and Berger, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Diffuse VN chromatin organisation is caused by the decondensation of pericentromeric heterochromatin, which involves the depletion of linker histone H1 and H3K9me2.
source: This is caused by the decondensation of pericentromeric heterochromatin, which involves the depletion of linker histone H1 and H3K9me2 (He et al., 2019; Mérai et al., 2014; Schoft et al., 2009; Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Heterochromatin decondensation licenses the active demethylation of pericentromeric DNA sequences by the gametophyte-specific DNA glycosylase DEMETER (DME).
source: Heterochromatin decondensation licenses the active demethylation of pericentromeric DNA sequences by the gametophyte-specific DNA glycosylase DEMETER (DME) (Andreuzza et al., 2010; He et al., 2019; Ibarra et al., 2012; Schoft et al., 2011), which stimulates transcription of transposable elements (TEs) and epigenetically activated small RNA (easiRNA) (Creasey et al., 2014; Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: DME-mediated DNA demethylation stimulates transcription of transposable elements (TEs) and epigenetically activated small RNA (easiRNA).
source: Heterochromatin decondensation licenses the active demethylation of pericentromeric DNA sequences by the gametophyte-specific DNA glycosylase DEMETER (DME) (Andreuzza et al., 2010; He et al., 2019; Ibarra et al., 2012; Schoft et al., 2011), which stimulates transcription of transposable elements (TEs) and epigenetically activated small RNA (easiRNA) (Creasey et al., 2014; Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The VN transcriptome strongly correlated with that of whole pollen but was poorly correlated with that of sperm.
source: Consistent with most pollen RNA deriving from the VC, the VN transcriptome strongly correlated with that of whole pollen but was poorly correlated with that of sperm (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C and D.

claim: The transcriptomes of two cells constituting mature pollen are highly distinct from each other and from transcriptomes of sporophytic cell types and tissues.
source: A principal component analysis illustrates how the transcriptomes of two cells constituting mature pollen are highly distinct from each other and from transcriptomes of sporophytic cell types and tissues (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by principal component analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Gene expression in haploid microspores was more related to diploid tissues of the sporophyte than to the two differentiated pollen cell types.
source: Gene expression in haploid microspores was more related to diploid tissues of the sporophyte than to the two differentiated pollen cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the principal component analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Major transcriptional reprogramming establishes distinct regulatory controls after unequal division of the microspore to specify the sperm and the VC.
source: This indicates that major transcriptional reprogramming establishes distinct regulatory controls after unequal division of the microspore to specify the sperm and the VC.
evidence: This is inferred from the transcriptome analysis and principal component analysis.

claim: Biological replicates for each stage were highly correlated, while modest cross-correlation between tissues indicated distinct chromatin landscapes.
source: First, biological replicates for each stage were highly correlated, while modest cross-correlation between tissues indicated distinct chromatin landscapes (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and C.

claim: ATAC-seq peaks were highly enriched at promoters.
source: Second, ATAC-seq peaks were highly enriched at promoters (Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claim: Highly transcribed genes showed higher accessibility around transcription start sites (TSSs) than genes with low expression.
source: Third, highly transcribed genes showed higher accessibility around transcription start sites (TSSs) than genes with low expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq signal distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: ATAC-seq profiles in SN and VN had characteristic periodicity arising from polynucleosome fragments.
source: Fourth, ATAC-seq profiles in SN and VN had characteristic periodicity arising from polynucleosome fragments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Supported by fragment size distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: No periodicity was evident in profiles from microspore nuclei (MN) and GN.
source: Although no periodicity was evident in profiles from microspore nuclei (MN) and GN (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D), we observed substantial overlap with profiles from other cell types as well as strong correlation of chromatin accessibility with active genes in the microspore and sperm, respectively (Figure 1C and D; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by fragment size distribution analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3D.

claim: A total of 20,634 ATAC-seq peaks covering over 15 Mb of the Arabidopsis genome were identified.
source: We identified a total of 20,634 ATAC-seq peaks covering over 15 Mb of the Arabidopsis genome (Figure 1C; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct result from the ATAC-seq peak calling analysis.

claim: Chromatin accessibility in microspores, differentiated pollen cell types, and seedlings strongly overlapped (15,982 peaks, 77.5%).
source: Chromatin accessibility in microspores, differentiated pollen cell types, and seedlings strongly overlapped (15,982 peaks, 77.5%) (Figure 1C–E).
evidence: Supported by peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: Common peaks were associated with genes involved in core housekeeping functions that maintain expression across the entire life cycle, such as mRNA metabolism, protein transport, cell cycle control, and osmotic stress response.
source: These common peaks were associated with genes involved in core housekeeping functions that maintain expression across the entire life cycle, such as mRNA metabolism, protein transport, cell cycle control, and osmotic stress response (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: A set of sporophyte-specific ACRs (6.7%; 1375 peaks) remained accessible between seedlings and MN, had reduced accessibility in the GN, but later lost accessibility in the SN and VN.
source: A set of sporophyte-specific ACRs (6.7%; 1375 peaks) remained accessible between seedlings and MN, had reduced accessibility in the GN, but later lost accessibility in the SN and VN (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq heatmap analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Sporophyte-specific ACRs occurred at genes involved in photosynthesis and energy metabolism.
source: These occurred at genes involved in photosynthesis and energy metabolism (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C), which are dispensable in the short-lived haploid gametophyte since it derives resources from the host parental sporophyte.
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: Photosynthesis and energy metabolism genes are dispensable in the short-lived haploid gametophyte since it derives resources from the host parental sporophyte.
source: These occurred at genes involved in photosynthesis and energy metabolism (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C), which are dispensable in the short-lived haploid gametophyte since it derives resources from the host parental sporophyte.
evidence: This is an inference based on the biological relationship between gametophyte and sporophyte.

claim: The analysis did not reveal de novo gains in chromatin accessibility in GN compared with MN but rather a gradual loss in accessibility among sporophytic-specific ACRs.
source: Our analysis did not reveal de novo gains in chromatin accessibility in GN compared with MN but rather a gradual loss in accessibility among sporophytic-specific ACRs (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq heatmap analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Pairwise comparisons between the pollen cell types revealed a gradual increase in differential accessibility across pollen development.
source: Pairwise comparisons between the pollen cell types revealed a gradual increase in differential accessibility across pollen development (Figure 1F; Figure 1—figure supplement 3E; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by differential ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Differences in chromatin accessibility were most pronounced at the mature pollen stage, with 6.8% (1400 peaks) and 9.1% (1877 peaks) cell type-specific ACRs unique to SN or VN, respectively.
source: These differences were most pronounced at the mature pollen stage, with 6.8% (1400 peaks) and 9.1% (1877 peaks) cell type-specific ACRs unique to SN or VN, respectively (Figure 1C–E; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by differential ATAC-seq analysis shown in Figure 1C-E.

claim: VN-specific ACRs were strongly associated with functions unique to pollen biology such as pollination, cell tip growth, and morphogenesis.
source: VN-specific ACRs were strongly associated with functions unique to pollen biology such as pollination, cell tip growth, and morphogenesis (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C).
evidence: Supported by gene ontology enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4C.

claim: High promoter accessibility was observed at genes directly regulated by DUO POLLEN 1 (DUO1) in sperm.
source: In sperm, we observed high promoter accessibility at genes directly regulated by DUO POLLEN 1 (DUO1), an essential R2R3-type MYB TF that controls sperm differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D; Borg et al., 2011; Brownfield et al., 2009; Rotman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq enrichment analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4D.

claim: DUO1 is an essential R2R3-type MYB TF that controls sperm differentiation.
source: In sperm, we observed high promoter accessibility at genes directly regulated by DUO POLLEN 1 (DUO1), an essential R2R3-type MYB TF that controls sperm differentiation (Figure 1—figure supplement 4D; Borg et al., 2011; Brownfield et al., 2009; Rotman et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The relative accessibility of promoter regions was positively correlated (R = 0.61) with differential expression of the associated genes between sperm and the VN.
source: Importantly, the relative accessibility of promoter regions was positively correlated (R = 0.61) with differential expression of the associated genes between sperm and the VN (Figure 1G), consistent with the distinct transcriptional state of each cell type.
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 1G.

claim: SN-specific and VN-specific ACRs were less prevalent at promoters but had an increased incidence within distal intergenic regions compared with common ACRs.
source: SN-specific and VN-specific ACRs were less prevalent at promoters but had an increased incidence within distal intergenic regions compared with common ACRs (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Transcribed genes most proximal to intergenic ACRs were differentially expressed in a cell type-specific manner.
source: Transcribed genes most proximal to these intergenic ACRs were differentially expressed in a cell type-specific manner (Figure 1—figure supplement 4E), suggesting distal regulatory influence.
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4E.

claim: VN-specific ACRs were highly enriched at transcriptional termination sites (TTSs) compared to other ACRs.
source: VN-specific ACRs were also highly enriched at transcriptional termination sites (TTSs) compared to other ACRs (Figure 1H; Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
evidence: Supported by genomic distribution analysis shown in Figure 1H and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claim: ATAC-seq peak density was reduced within pericentromeric regions compared to the arms of each of the five Arabidopsis chromosomes.
source: ATAC-seq peak density was reduced within pericentromeric regions compared to the arms of each of the five Arabidopsis chromosomes (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by chromosomal distribution analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: There was a slight but consistent increase in ATAC-seq peak density within pericentromeric regions of the VN compared to SN.
source: We also noted a slight but consistent increase in ATAC-seq peak density within pericentromeric regions of the VN compared to SN (Figure 2A; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by chromosomal distribution analysis shown in Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: VN-specific ACRs were relatively enriched for H3K9me2 in somatic tissues but depleted for active H3K4me3 and H3K27ac histone marks.
source: Consistent with this, and unlike common or SN-specific ACRs, VN-specific ACRs were relatively enriched for H3K9me2 in somatic tissues but depleted for active H3K4me3 and H3K27ac histone marks, with just over one-third (36.5%; 686 peaks) marked by H3K9me2 in leaves (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2B, C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Just over one-third (36.5%; 686 peaks) of VN-specific ACRs were marked by H3K9me2 in leaves.
source: Consistent with this, and unlike common or SN-specific ACRs, VN-specific ACRs were relatively enriched for H3K9me2 in somatic tissues but depleted for active H3K4me3 and H3K27ac histone marks, with just over one-third (36.5%; 686 peaks) marked by H3K9me2 in leaves (Figure 2B and C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from ChIP-seq enrichment analysis.

claim: Almost one-third of VN-specific ACRs significantly overlapped with a TE insertion.
source: Similarly, almost one-third of VN-specific ACRs significantly overlapped with a TE insertion (Figure 2D and E), with DNA/MuDR and LINE/L1 elements notably over-represented (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2D and E.

claim: DNA/MuDR and LINE/L1 elements were notably over-represented among VN-specific ACRs overlapping with TEs.
source: Similarly, almost one-third of VN-specific ACRs significantly overlapped with a TE insertion (Figure 2D and E), with DNA/MuDR and LINE/L1 elements notably over-represented (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by TE family distribution analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: TEs specifically activated in pollen showed increased promoter accessibility specifically in the VN.
source: Accordingly, TEs specifically activated in pollen showed increased promoter accessibility specifically in the VN (Figure 2G; He et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: VN-specific ACRs were significantly associated with regions that produce pollen siRNAs, including 21–22-nt class easiRNAs known to preferentially accumulate in pollen.
source: VN-specific ACRs were also significantly associated with regions that produce pollen siRNAs, including 21–22-nt class easiRNAs known to preferentially accumulate in pollen (Figure 2C and D; Borges et al., 2018; Martinez et al., 2018; Slotkin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C and D, and citations to previous research.

claim: VN-specific ACRs (982 peaks; 52.3%) contained DME-dependent hypermethylated cytosines.
source: Strikingly, VN-specific ACRs were significantly enriched for regions demethylated by DME in the VN (Figure 2C and D), with just over half of all VN-specific ACRs (982 peaks; 52.3%) containing DME-dependent hypermethylated cytosines (Figure 3A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from differential methylation analysis.

claim: A small fraction of common ACRs were also targeted for demethylation (2052 peaks; 12.8%).
source: A small fraction of common ACRs were also targeted for demethylation (2052 peaks; 12.8%) (Figure 3B; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from differential methylation analysis.

claim: DME mediates demethylation in all cytosine contexts of the VN.
source: Metaplots centred over DME-targeted ACRs illustrate the demethylation mediated by DME in all cytosine contexts of the VN (Figure 3D), which is mirrored by higher levels of chromatin accessibility in the VN than in SN (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation metaplots shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Higher levels of chromatin accessibility in the VN than in SN mirror DME-mediated demethylation.
source: Metaplots centred over DME-targeted ACRs illustrate the demethylation mediated by DME in all cytosine contexts of the VN (Figure 3D), which is mirrored by higher levels of chromatin accessibility in the VN than in SN (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq metaplots shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The levels of DNA methylation remained unchanged over DME-targeted ACRs in WT and dme-2/+ sperm.
source: Consistent with the VN-specific expression and activity of DME (Park et al., 2017), the levels of DNA methylation remained unchanged over these regions in WT and dme-2/+ sperm.
evidence: This is inferred from the DNA methylation data and is consistent with VN-specific DME expression.

claim: DME activity is unlikely to stimulate a gain in chromatin accessibility alone, at least at common ACRs, but rather modulates differential DNA methylation levels within these shared open chromatin sites.
source: DME activity is thus unlikely to stimulate a gain in chromatin accessibility alone, at least at common ACRs, but rather modulates differential DNA methylation levels within these shared open chromatin sites.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that common ACRs are accessible in both cell types but have differential methylation.

claim: Chromatin accessibility likely precedes DME activity, consistent with the requirement of histone H1 depletion for DNA demethylation in the VN.
source: This suggests that chromatin accessibility likely precedes DME activity, consistent with the requirement of histone H1 depletion for DNA demethylation in the VN (He et al., 2019).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Fifty TFs expressed in the VN were present in the DAP-seq database, of which two-thirds (36 of 50; 72.0%) had significantly enriched motifs within DME-targeted ACRs.
source: Fifty TFs expressed in the VN were present in the DAP-seq database, of which two-thirds (36 of 50; 72.0%) had significantly enriched motifs within DME-targeted ACRs (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from motif enrichment analysis.

claim: Motifs bound by MYB101 were enriched within DME-targeted ACRs.
source: These included motifs bound by MYB101 (Figure 3E), a pollen-specific TF that acts redundantly with MYB97 and MYB120 to regulate pollen tube growth (Leydon et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by motif enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E and citations to previous research.

claim: MYB101 is a pollen-specific TF that acts redundantly with MYB97 and MYB120 to regulate pollen tube growth.
source: These included motifs bound by MYB101 (Figure 3E), a pollen-specific TF that acts redundantly with MYB97 and MYB120 to regulate pollen tube growth (Leydon et al., 2013; Liang et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The binding affinity of most TFs in Arabidopsis is strongly inhibited by DNA methylation.
source: The binding affinity of most TFs in Arabidopsis is strongly inhibited by DNA methylation, which was determined by performing the DAP-seq assay with methylated (DAP) or non-methylated (ampDAP) DNA (O'Malley et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research using DAP-seq and ampDAP-seq.

claim: Of the 36 TFs predicted to bind within DME-targeted ACRs, 25 had been assessed for methylation sensitivity, half of which (14 of 25; 56.0%) were inhibited by DNA methylation.
source: Of the 36 TFs predicted to bind within DME-targeted ACRs, 25 had been assessed in this manner (O'Malley et al., 2016), half of which (14 of 25; 56.0%) were inhibited by DNA methylation (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from analysis of DAP-seq data.

claim: DNA demethylation by DME facilitates the binding of several methylation-sensitive TFs within DME-targeted ACRs.
source: This suggests that DNA demethylation by DME facilitates the binding of several methylation-sensitive TFs within DME-targeted ACRs.
evidence: This is inferred from the enrichment of methylation-sensitive TF motifs in DME-targeted ACRs.

claim: The predicted binding sites for methylation-sensitive TFs were substantially hypo-methylated in VN from WT pollen.
source: Consistently, the predicted binding sites for these methylation-sensitive TFs were substantially hypo-methylated in VN from WT pollen (Figure 3G–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation analysis shown in Figure 3G-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J.

claim: In dme-2/+ mutant pollen, predicted TF binding sites were hyper-methylated to around half of the levels in WT sperm.
source: In dme-2/+ mutant pollen, these predicted binding sites were hyper-methylated to around half of the levels in WT sperm, consistent with the heterozygous nature of the dme-2 mutant (Figure 3G–J; Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–J).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation analysis shown in Figure 3G-J and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A-J.

claim: DME-targeted ACRs clustered into two groups distinguished by a relative enrichment or depletion of H3K9me2, H3K27me1, and histone H1 in sporophytic tissue.
source: DME-targeted ACRs clustered into two groups distinguished by a relative enrichment or depletion of H3K9me2, H3K27me1, and histone H1 in sporophytic tissue (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by clustering analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: DME activity in open chromatin targets the genome uniformly in both pericentromeric regions and chromosome arms.
source: DME activity in open chromatin thus targets the genome uniformly in both pericentromeric regions and chromosome arms (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Supported by chromosomal distribution analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The 3034 DME-targeted ACRs were strongly enriched for TEs and for regions that produce siRNAs.
source: The 3034 DME-targeted ACRs were strongly enriched for TEs and for regions that produce siRNAs (Figure 2C and D), with around one-fifth (661 peaks, 21.8%) lying distally within intergenic regions (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: Around one-fifth (661 peaks, 21.8%) of DME-targeted ACRs lie distally within intergenic regions.
source: The 3034 DME-targeted ACRs were strongly enriched for TEs and for regions that produce siRNAs (Figure 2C and D), with around one-fifth (661 peaks, 21.8%) lying distally within intergenic regions (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genomic distribution analysis.

claim: The majority of DME-targeted ACRs (2373 peaks, 78.2%) lie in the vicinity of protein-coding genes.
source: However, the majority of DME-targeted ACRs (2373 peaks, 78.2.8%) lied in the vicinity of protein-coding genes (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 3), which were significantly over-represented amongst VN-expressed genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genomic distribution analysis.

claim: Genes with a DME-targeted ACR were significantly over-represented amongst VN-expressed genes.
source: However, the majority of DME-targeted ACRs (2373 peaks, 78.2.8%) lied in the vicinity of protein-coding genes (Figure 4A; Supplementary file 3), which were significantly over-represented amongst VN-expressed genes (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There was a small but highly significant overlap between genes with a DME-targeted ACR and genes differentially expressed in dme-2/+ mutant pollen.
source: Importantly, we observed a small but highly significant overlap between genes with a DME-targeted ACR and genes differentially expressed in dme-2/+ mutant pollen (Figure 4C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), confirming that DME directly modulates gene expression during pollen development.
evidence: Supported by overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4C, D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: DME directly modulates gene expression during pollen development.
source: Importantly, we observed a small but highly significant overlap between genes with a DME-targeted ACR and genes differentially expressed in dme-2/+ mutant pollen (Figure 4C and D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), confirming that DME directly modulates gene expression during pollen development.
evidence: This is inferred from the significant overlap between DME-targeted ACRs and differentially expressed genes in dme mutants.

claim: The 27 genes with a DME-targeted ACR and differentially expressed in dme-2/+ mutant pollen included protein kinases, cysteine-rich peptides, metabolic proteins, as well as transcription factors.
source: These 27 genes included protein kinases, cysteine-rich peptides, metabolic proteins, as well as transcription factors, gene functions that are all known to be involved in pollen tube growth (Figure 4D; Supplementary file 4; Supplementary file 5; Higashiyama and Takeuchi, 2015; Qu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a direct result from the overlap analysis and gene annotation.

claim: Protein kinases, cysteine-rich peptides, metabolic proteins, and transcription factors are all known to be involved in pollen tube growth.
source: These 27 genes included protein kinases, cysteine-rich peptides, metabolic proteins, as well as transcription factors, gene functions that are all known to be involved in pollen tube growth (Figure 4D; Supplementary file 4; Supplementary file 5; Higashiyama and Takeuchi, 2015; Qu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on pollen tube growth.

claim: RFK2 was the most significantly downregulated gene in dme-2/+ pollen.
source: The most significantly downregulated gene in dme-2/+ pollen was a pollen-specific cysteine-rich RECEPTOR-LIKE SERINE/THREONINE KINASE (RFK2) (Figure 4C), which is embedded within H3K9me2-marked heterochromatin in the sporophyte (Figure 4E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: RFK2 is embedded within H3K9me2-marked heterochromatin in the sporophyte.
source: The most significantly downregulated gene in dme-2/+ pollen was a pollen-specific cysteine-rich RECEPTOR-LIKE SERINE/THREONINE KINASE (RFK2) (Figure 4C), which is embedded within H3K9me2-marked heterochromatin in the sporophyte (Figure 4E; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 4E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The upstream promoter region of RFK2 was heavily hypomethylated in VN from WT pollen and contained several DME-demethylated cytosines including at predicted binding sites for bZIP2, ERF3, and ERF8.
source: The upstream promoter region of RFK2 was heavily hypomethylated in VN from WT pollen and contained several DME-demethylated cytosines including at predicted binding sites for bZIP2, ERF3, and ERF8 (Figure 4E), three DNA methylation-sensitive TFs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by DNA methylation and motif analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 3F.

claim: bZIP2, ERF3, and ERF8 are DNA methylation-sensitive TFs.
source: The upstream promoter region of RFK2 was heavily hypomethylated in VN from WT pollen and contained several DME-demethylated cytosines including at predicted binding sites for bZIP2, ERF3, and ERF8 (Figure 4E), three DNA methylation-sensitive TFs (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by DAP-seq analysis shown in Figure 3F.

claim: DME-targeted ACRs were significantly associated with genes upregulated in growing pollen tubes.
source: Interestingly, DME-targeted ACRs were significantly associated with genes upregulated in growing pollen tubes, which occurs upon interaction of semi in vivo grown pollen tubes (SIVPT) with female pistil tissue (Figure 4B, SIVPT-induced) (Leydon et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 4B and citations to previous research.

claim: 352 genes associated with DME-targeted ACRs encode several examples of well-characterised pollen-specific receptor like-kinases, calcium-dependent protein kinases, cation/H+ exchanger proteins, and RALF-like signalling peptides.
source: These 352 genes encode several examples of well-characterised pollen-specific receptor like-kinases, calcium-dependent protein kinases, cation/H+ exchanger proteins, and RALF-like signalling peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, grey labels) (Myers et al., 2009; Sze et al., 2004; Takeuchi and Higashiyama, 2016), around a quarter of which had little to no transcripts detectable in dry pollen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by gene annotation and expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and 1F, and citations to previous research.

claim: Around a quarter of the 352 genes associated with DME-targeted ACRs and upregulated in growing pollen tubes had little to no transcripts detectable in dry pollen.
source: These 352 genes encode several examples of well-characterised pollen-specific receptor like-kinases, calcium-dependent protein kinases, cation/H+ exchanger proteins, and RALF-like signalling peptides (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, grey labels) (Myers et al., 2009; Sze et al., 2004; Takeuchi and Higashiyama, 2016), around a quarter of which had little to no transcripts detectable in dry pollen (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1F.

claim: DME demethylation acts to poise cis-regulatory regions for the onset of events taking place after pollination to facilitate the de novo wave of gene expression that occurs in the growing pollen tube.
source: Thus, DME demethylation acts to poise cis-regulatory regions for the onset of events taking place after pollination to facilitate the de novo wave of gene expression that occurs in the growing pollen tube (Leydon et al., 2017; Qin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the association of DME-targeted ACRs with genes upregulated during pollen tube growth.

claim: Sperm chromatin is epigenetically reprogrammed through the global loss of H3K27me3, which involves the sperm-specific deposition of histone H3.10 and active demethylation by Jumonji-C family H3K27 demethylases EARLY FLOWERING 6 (ELF6), RELATIVE OF ELF6 (REF6), and JUMONJI 13 (JMJ13).
source: In Arabidopsis, sperm chromatin is epigenetically reprogrammed through the global loss of H3K27me3, which involves the sperm-specific deposition of histone H3.10 and active demethylation by Jumonji-C family H3K27 demethylases EARLY FLOWERING 6 (ELF6), RELATIVE OF ELF6 (REF6), and JUMONJI 13 (JMJ13) (Borg et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The global loss of H3K27me3 in sperm is accompanied by selective priming with or without H3K4me3.
source: We previously showed that the global loss of H3K27me3 in sperm is accompanied by selective priming with or without H3K4me3 (Borg et al., 2020; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: H3K4me3-primed genes were marked by increased chromatin accessibility in their flanking promoter region and were enriched for SN-specific ACRs.
source: Consistently, H3K4me3-primed genes were marked by increased chromatin accessibility in their flanking promoter region and were enriched for SN-specific ACRs (Figure 5A and B, primed cluster).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq and overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: SN-specific ACRs were depleted for active marks in sporophytic leaf tissue but highly enriched for H3K27me3.
source: SN-specific ACRs were depleted for active marks in sporophytic leaf tissue but highly enriched for H3K27me3 (Figure 5C; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Almost one half of the SN-specific ACRs (627; 44.8%) overlapped a sporophytic H3K27me3 domain.
source: Almost one half of the SN-specific ACRs (627; 44.8%) overlapped a sporophytic H3K27me3 domain (Figure 5D; Supplementary file 6).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from overlap analysis.

claim: The remaining SN-specific ACRs (773; 55.2%) lacked H3K27me3 in the sporophyte, suggesting sporophytic repression by an unknown pathway.
source: The remaining SN-specific ACRs (773; 55.2%) lacked H3K27me3 in the sporophyte (Figure 5D; Supplementary file 6), suggesting sporophytic repression by an unknown pathway.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from overlap analysis, with the suggestion of unknown repression being speculative.

claim: The majority of SN-specific ACRs (1044 peaks; 74.6%) were associated with a protein-coding gene.
source: The majority of SN-specific ACRs (1044 peaks; 74.6%) were associated with a protein-coding gene (Figure 5E), around one-third of which were significantly over-represented for sperm-expressed genes (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from genomic distribution analysis.

claim: Around one-third of genes associated with SN-specific ACRs were significantly over-represented for sperm-expressed genes.
source: The majority of SN-specific ACRs (1044 peaks; 74.6%) were associated with a protein-coding gene (Figure 5E), around one-third of which were significantly over-represented for sperm-expressed genes (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: SN-specific ACRs include several direct DUO1 target genes, including DUO1-ACTIVATED ZINC FINGER (DAZ3) and PLANT CADMIUM RESISTANCE 11 (PCR11), as well as the paternally transcribed embryonic regulator SHORT SUSPENSOR (SSP).
source: These included several direct DUO1 target genes, including DUO1-ACTIVATED ZINC FINGER (DAZ3) and PLANT CADMIUM RESISTANCE 11 (PCR11), as well as the paternally transcribed embryonic regulator SHORT SUSPENSOR (SSP) (Figure 5G; Bayer et al., 2009; Borg et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5G and citations to previous research.

claim: Genes neighbouring H3K27me3-marked ACRs were significantly downregulated upon retention of H3K27me3, which occurs in mutant sperm compromised for the pathways that remove H3K27me3.
source: The genes neighbouring H3K27me3-marked ACRs were significantly downregulated upon retention of H3K27me3, which occurs in mutant sperm compromised for the pathways that remove H3K27me3 (Figure 5H; Borg et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5H and citation to previous work.

claim: H3K27me3 in GN remains comparable to levels in microspores but is specifically lost in divided sperm.
source: Incidentally, H3K27me3 in GN remains comparable to levels in microspores but is specifically lost in divided sperm (Borg et al., 2020), further supporting our observation that major reorganisation of chromatin accessibility in sperm coincides with H3K27me3 reprogramming.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Major reorganisation of chromatin accessibility in sperm coincides with H3K27me3 reprogramming.
source: Incidentally, H3K27me3 in GN remains comparable to levels in microspores but is specifically lost in divided sperm (Borg et al., 2020), further supporting our observation that major reorganisation of chromatin accessibility in sperm coincides with H3K27me3 reprogramming.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of H3K27me3 loss and chromatin accessibility changes.

claim: H3K27me3 reprogramming exposes cis-regulatory elements to the transcriptional machinery during sperm specification.
source: These results reveal how H3K27me3 reprogramming exposes cis-regulatory elements to the transcriptional machinery during sperm specification.
evidence: This is inferred from the association of H3K27me3-marked ACRs with sperm-expressed genes.

claim: One quarter of the H3K27me3-repressed ACRs (110 peaks; 27.0%) were associated with genes expressed specifically during the initiation of sporophytic development in the early embryo.
source: In addition to genes transcribed in sperm, one quarter of the H3K27me3-repressed ACRs (110 peaks; 27.0%) were also associated with genes expressed specifically during the initiation of sporophytic development in the early embryo (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from overlap enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Several master embryonic regulators all had high levels of chromatin accessibility in sperm, including BABY BOOM (BBM), LEAFY COTYLEDON 1 (LEC1), and WUSCHEL-RELATED HOMEOBOX 2 (WOX2), as well as the floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC).
source: Strikingly, several master embryonic regulators all had high levels of chromatin accessibility in sperm, including BABY BOOM (BBM), LEAFY COTYLEDON 1 (LEC1), and WUSCHEL-RELATED HOMEOBOX 2 (WOX2), as well as the floral repressor FLOWERING LOCUS C (FLC) (Figure 5I; Boscá et al., 2011; Horstman et al., 2017; Tao et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5I and citations to previous research.

claim: Genes with enriched expression during the early and middle phases of embryogenesis had higher levels of promoter accessibility than genes with enriched expression later during embryo maturation.
source: This trend was broadly evident at genes with enriched expression during the early and middle phases of embryogenesis, which had higher levels of promoter accessibility than genes with enriched expression later during embryo maturation (Figure 5J; Hofmann et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by ATAC-seq enrichment analysis shown in Figure 5J and citation to previous research.

claim: Sperm chromatin is highly derived from the gametophytic state observed in the VN, since it is distinguished by accessible chromatin that forecasts the sporophytic transition in the next generation.
source: Thus, sperm chromatin is highly derived from the gametophytic state observed in the VN, since it is distinguished by accessible chromatin that forecasts the sporophytic transition in the next generation.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that sperm have accessible chromatin at embryonic genes.

claim: Distinct epigenetic reprogramming events rewire transcription through major reorganisation of the regulatory epigenome during the alternation of generations in flowering plants.
source: Hence, distinct epigenetic reprogramming events rewire transcription through major reorganisation of the regulatory epigenome to guide the alternation of generations in flowering plants.
evidence: This is the main conclusion synthesized from all the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The programmed removal of H3K9 and DNA methylation in the VC facilitates the expression of a fraction of the genes required for somatic haploid development.
source: Once microspore division is complete, the programmed removal of H3K9 and DNA methylation in the VC facilitates the expression of a fraction of the genes required for somatic haploid development.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing loss of H3K9me2 and DNA methylation in VN and associated gene expression changes.

claim: H3K27me3 removal in sperm exposes cis-regulatory regions at developmental genes required to initiate transition back to diploid life after fertilisation.
source: In parallel, H3K27me3 removal in sperm exposes cis-regulatory regions at developmental genes required to initiate transition back to diploid life after fertilisation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing H3K27me3 loss in sperm and accessible chromatin at embryonic genes.

claim: Substantial differences in ACRs have been observed across sporophytic Arabidopsis tissues.
source: While substantial differences in ACRs have been observed across sporophytic Arabidopsis tissues (Sullivan et al., 2014), more closely related cell types appear to show few specific open chromatin sites (Dorrity et al., 2020; Maher et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: More closely related cell types appear to show few specific open chromatin sites.
source: While substantial differences in ACRs have been observed across sporophytic Arabidopsis tissues (Sullivan et al., 2014), more closely related cell types appear to show few specific open chromatin sites (Dorrity et al., 2020; Maher et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Thousands of differential ACRs distinguish the SN and VN, despite being separated by a single cell division.
source: Despite being separated by a single cell division, thousands of differential ACRs distinguish the SN and VN, which is the result of the epigenetic reprogramming that occur across the male sporophyte-to-gametophyte transition.
evidence: This is a direct result from the differential ATAC-seq analysis.

claim: The epigenetic reprogramming events underlying the male haploid transition likely trace back to ancient, conserved mechanisms that accompany life form transitions in early land plants.
source: The epigenetic reprogramming events underlying the male haploid transition likely trace back to ancient, conserved mechanisms that accompany life form transitions in early land plants (Ikeda et al., 2018; Okano et al., 2009; Schmid et al., 2018; Yaari et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on evolutionary considerations and citations to previous research.

claim: Alternating haploid–diploid life forms in eukaryotes are likely derived from the dominant haploid phase of ancestral unicellular organisms.
source: Alternating haploid–diploid life forms in eukaryotes are likely derived from the dominant haploid phase of ancestral unicellular organisms (Niklas et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous evolutionary research.

claim: Multicellularity is proposed to have evolved in haploid organisms first and was then followed by meiosis to mitigate spontaneous whole-genome duplications.
source: Multicellularity is proposed to have evolved in these haploid organisms first and was then followed by meiosis to mitigate spontaneous whole-genome duplications (Lenormand et al., 2016; Niklas et al., 2014; Wilkins and Holliday, 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous evolutionary research.

claim: H3K27me3 likely evolved in unicellular eukaryotes prior to the repressive feedback loop that couples DNA with H3K9 methylation in land plants.
source: H3K27me3 likely evolved in unicellular eukaryotes prior to the repressive feedback loop that couples DNA with H3K9 methylation in land plants (Bewick et al., 2017; Schuettengruber et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous evolutionary research.

claim: H3K27me3 reprogramming at the haploid-to-diploid transition might be a remnant of an ancestral role in the first haplo-diplo phasic life cycles.
source: We propose that H3K27me3 reprogramming at the haploid-to-diploid transition might be a remnant of an ancestral role in the first haplo-diplo phasic life cycles.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on evolutionary considerations.

claim: The DNA-H3K9 methylation feedback loop might have been co-opted to control diploid-to-haploid life form transitions during early land plant evolution.
source: We also postulate that the DNA-H3K9 methylation feedback loop, which is normally associated with transposon silencing in flowering plants (Feng and Michaels, 2015), might have been co-opted to control diploid-to-haploid life form transitions during early land plant evolution.
evidence: This is a speculative postulate based on the findings and evolutionary considerations.

claim: H3K9 methylation is implicated in the transcriptional repression of not only transposons but also lineage specification in flowering plants.
source: Importantly, our findings implicate H3K9 methylation in the transcriptional repression of not only transposons but also lineage specification in flowering plants, which has developmental relevance during early mouse organogenesis (Nicetto et al., 2019) but likely also in the specification of the female gametophyte (Jiang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is inferred from the findings and supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The reprogramming and demethylation of pericentromeric heterochromatin are primarily required for VC differentiation.
source: Our findings suggest that the reprogramming and demethylation of pericentromeric heterochromatin are primarily required for VC differentiation.
evidence: This is inferred from the data showing loss of heterochromatin and DNA demethylation in VN.

claim: DME is essential for pollen viability and pollen tube germination in certain Arabidopsis ecotypes.
source: DME is essential for pollen viability and pollen tube germination in certain Arabidopsis ecotypes (Schoft et al., 2011), which is consistent with our findings that DME regulates the expression of several pollen tube-related genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Physical proximity of the promoter and terminator through intragenic looping often facilitates rapid re-initiation of transcription.
source: Physical proximity of the promoter and terminator through intragenic looping often facilitates rapid re-initiation of transcription (Grzechnik et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Insulating proteins at 3' ends might prevent transcriptional read-through into neighbouring genes.
source: Alternatively, these regions might be occupied by insulating proteins that prevent transcriptional read-through into neighbouring genes (West et al., 2002).
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation supported by citation to previous research.

claim: DME-dependent demethylation preferentially targets short AT-rich TEs.
source: DME-dependent demethylation preferentially targets short AT-rich TEs (Ibarra et al., 2012), suggesting that gametophytic development is at least partly specified through de-repression of TE-associated cis-regulatory sequences.
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: Gametophytic development is at least partly specified through de-repression of TE-associated cis-regulatory sequences.
source: DME-dependent demethylation preferentially targets short AT-rich TEs (Ibarra et al., 2012), suggesting that gametophytic development is at least partly specified through de-repression of TE-associated cis-regulatory sequences.
evidence: This is inferred from the preferential targeting of TEs by DME and the association with gametophytic genes.

claim: Rewiring of gene expression by transposons and endogenous retroviruses is proposed to have contributed to the evolution and diversification of mammals.
source: Rewiring of gene expression by transposons and endogenous retroviruses is proposed to have contributed to the evolution and diversification of mammals (Johnson, 2019; Lynch et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: During early embryogenesis in mice and humans, accessible chromatin is widely shaped by fixed TE insertions that strongly associate with cis-regulatory elements.
source: During early embryogenesis in mice and humans, accessible chromatin is widely shaped by fixed TE insertions that strongly associate with cis-regulatory elements (Wu et al., 2016; Wu et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Novel TE and endovirus integrations can create novel promoters or TF binding sites that alter the regulation of nearby or even distant genes.
source: Novel TE and endovirus integrations can create novel promoters or TF binding sites that alter the regulation of nearby or even distant genes (Rebollo et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous research.

claim: TE integrations may have imposed repression on the gametophytic programme during diploid life, which in turn could have facilitated the evolution of haploid–diploid life cycles in land plants.
source: We speculate whether TE integrations have imposed repression on the gametophytic programme during diploid life, which in turn could have facilitated the evolution of haploid–diploid life cycles in land plants.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the findings.

claim: The fixation and selection of transposon-derived cis-regulatory elements marks specific periods of evolution within a lineage.
source: This hypothesis supports the general proposal that the fixation and selection of transposon-derived cis-regulatory elements marks specific periods of evolution within a lineage (Jacques et al., 2013; Jordan et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous evolutionary research.
